date: 2026-04-11

slug: "local-development-workflow-you-can-keep"

Ahnii!

If you want a local workflow that is easy to start, easy to share, and hard to break, this post shows you how to combine [DDEV](https://ddev.readthedocs.io/), [Git](https://git-scm.com/), [Just](https://github.com/casey/just), and [direnv](https://direnv.net/) into one repeatable setup.

## Prerequisites

- A project tracked in Git
- Docker running on your machine
- DDEV installed
- Just installed
- direnv installed

## Build One Entry Point For Daily Work

A good workflow starts with one obvious command surface, but that only helps if every common task lives there.

```make
set shell := ["bash", "-lc"]

start:
    ddev start

stop:
    ddev stop

test:
    ddev exec php artisan test

lint:
    ddev exec ./vendor/bin/pint

queue:
    ddev exec php artisan queue:work

fresh:
    ddev exec php artisan migrate:fresh --seed
```

This `justfile` gives you one place to start, stop, test, lint, and reset the project. You stop remembering container commands and start using task names your team can share.

If your commands are still scattered across shell history, the next fix is to make the environment load itself.

## Load Project Environment Variables Automatically

Your workflow slows down when every terminal tab starts empty, but you can remove that friction with one small file.

```bash
export APP_ENV=local
export LOG_LEVEL=debug
export FORCE_COLOR=1
layout bash
```

This `.envrc` file loads project-specific environment values as soon as you enter the directory. It keeps local defaults local, which matters once you start moving between projects in the same day.

After that, allow the file once:

```bash
direnv allow
```

This tells direnv to trust the current `.envrc`. From then on, your shell picks up the right values automatically when you `cd` into the project.

Now your commands and environment are stable, but the workflow gets clearer when you can see how the pieces connect.

## See The Workflow As A System

A local workflow is easier to maintain when you treat it like a pipeline instead of a pile of commands.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Open project directory] --> B[direnv loads local environment]
    B --> C[Run just command]
    C --> D[DDEV starts or executes inside containers]
    D --> E[App code, tests, and services run consistently]
    E --> F[Git records changes in a predictable repo state]
```

This flow keeps each tool in a narrow role. `direnv` sets the shell, `just` gives you task names, `DDEV` runs the app, and `Git` tracks the result.

Once the pieces have clear jobs, you can tighten the daily loop.

## Run A Daily Loop You Do Not Need To Rethink

You do not need a clever workflow. You need one that feels the same every morning.

```bash
just start
just test
just lint
git status
```

This sequence brings the project up, checks behavior, checks style, and shows you what changed. It is short enough to remember, which is why it tends to survive.

If you want to make that loop even harder to skip, add one command that runs the full pre-commit check.

```make
check:
    just test
    just lint
    git diff --quiet
```

This `check` task gives you one gate before commit or push. It also makes the workflow easier to teach because you can point people to a single command instead of a checklist.

That covers the happy path, but a workflow is only useful if you can tell when it is actually working.

## Verify The Workflow Works On A Clean Pull

The fastest way to find workflow gaps is to act like you have never seen the project before.

```bash
git pull
just start
just test
```

If these commands work on a clean pull, your workflow is probably in good shape. If they fail, the missing step is the thing you should automate next.

{{< callout type="tip" >}}
If a setup step only exists in your memory, it is not part of the workflow yet. Put it in `justfile`, `.envrc`, or project docs.
{{< /callout >}}

The last part is not another tool. It is the rule that keeps this setup from drifting.

## Keep The Workflow Small Enough To Trust

Add tools only when they remove a repeated decision. If a new layer gives you more setup, more exceptions, or more local-only knowledge, cut it.

A stable local workflow usually has three traits: one command entry point, one reproducible runtime, and one obvious verification path. Once you have that, you can scale the project without rebuilding your habits every week.

# Project Name

You use this repository to install the package, run the app locally, and start building without extra setup.

## Install The Project

```bash
git clone https://github.com/your-org/your-repo.git
cd your-repo
composer install
```

You clone the repository and install PHP dependencies with [Composer](https://getcomposer.org/). This gives you a working local copy with the packages the project needs.

## Configure Your Environment

```bash
cp .env.example .env
php artisan key:generate
```

You create your local environment file and generate the application key. This gives you a safe default config for local development.

## Run The App Locally

```bash
php artisan serve
```

You start the local development server. Open the URL shown in your terminal to confirm the app is running.

## Use The Main Development Commands

```bash
php artisan test
php artisan migrate
```

You run the test suite with the first command. You apply database migrations with the second.

## Start Making Changes

Make one change at a time.

Run tests after each change.

Keep the README current when setup or usage changes.
